text: The Fleet Has Set Sail, So Why Does the Old Man Still Protest from Shore? Who May Say a Community's Glory Costs Too Much?
The fleet lies on the waters outside Lisbon.
Its flags unfurl in the wind.
The soldiers and sailors are ready.
They pray for the voyage ahead and prepare their souls to face death.
For everyone knows that the open sea is no road already laid.
On shore, however, the scene is different.
The people of the city gather by the sea.
Some have come to see off friends.
Some have come to see off family.
Others simply want to watch the fleet depart.
A mother asks through her tears:
You are my only comfort in old age. Why go somewhere that may make a fish's belly your grave?
A wife asks:
Why surrender this life that belongs to our life together to the raging sea?
Old people and children follow in the crowd too.
Tears wet the white sand.
Those departing do not look up at their mothers and wives.
The narrator says they fear that pain will shake their resolve and change the purpose they have already settled on.
So they forgo the customary farewells and board the ships directly.
Just as the fleet begins to leave the shore, an old man raises his voice.
The Lusiads is an epic celebrating Portuguese navigation, warfare, discovery, and national achievement.
Da Gama's fleet will sail toward India.
The ocean will be crossed.
New routes, knowledge, trade, and imperial spaces will open up through this expedition.
If the old man appeared only in a later work opposing ocean voyages, his words would be unremarkable.
What is remarkable is that he stands at the very scene of departure in this epic of glory.
The fleet's preparations are complete.
The prayers have been offered.
The young men are fired with enthusiasm for a great undertaking.
Yet the poem places an old man whose “wisdom comes from experience alone” among the crowd, shaking his head three times.
His voice is grave, yet loud enough to be heard clearly by those already on the water.
He has not prevailed in the decision.
But even as that decision is being carried out, he is allowed to leave his opposition in the song.
The old man's first target is not the ships.
It is the names people give their desires.
He cries out:
The glory of dominion.
The vanity called fame.
The pleasure kindled by public approval and called honor.
Then he asks:
How many people will these splendid names expose to death, danger, storms, and cruelty?
And what costs will they bring this country and its people with their promises of kingdoms, gold mines, victories, triumphs, and a place in history?
This succession of questions does not prove that “glory” is merely a lie.
Some actions truly deserve remembrance.
Crossing into the unknown takes courage.
A community can also gain real capabilities through public undertakings.
What the old man attacks is the way a name can settle a judgment in advance.
Once an expedition is called a great undertaking, its opponents can easily be called cowards.
Once a desire is called national glory, those who bear its cost seem already to have agreed.
If the future will find its place in heroic history, the crying before us seems merely the weakness of those unable to grasp the great purpose ahead.
Nor are those aboard the fleet paying no price.
They are not sitting somewhere safe, ordering others to die in their place.
The poem explicitly says that they keep death before their eyes and leave the shore with misgivings too.
The dangers at sea fall first upon the voyagers' own bodies.
We therefore cannot make the old man the only person who sees the value of life, or portray the sailors as driven solely by gold and vanity.
Someone can know they may die and still be willing to set out.
A willingness to risk oneself for knowledge, a mission, a country, or a name does not in itself mean losing the capacity for judgment.
But the voyagers' willingness to pay does not mean that they alone will pay every cost.
Mothers lose their support in old age.
Wives lose the people with whom they share their lives.
Children lose care and companionship.
The country may lose people, wealth, and defensive strength.
People far away will also face the consequences of contact, trade, occupation, or attack, though they have not yet appeared in this farewell on the shore.
An undertaking in which the bravest take the risks themselves does not thereby belong to them alone.
The wife on shore says:
The life you venture on the sea is mine too, not yours alone.
Taken without limit, this statement creates problems too.
No intimate relationship can make one person's life entirely another's property.
A wife cannot acquire the right to decide her husband's entire future merely because she will grieve.
A mother cannot make it impossible for her son ever to leave merely because he is her support in old age.
Nor can children's needs mean that their parents must henceforth choose only the least risky life.
Otherwise, love would keep everyone who shares a life on shore.
Yet “your life does not belong to you alone” can also express a narrower fact:
Through your relationships, your decision has already entered other people's lives.
You may still decide to leave.
You cannot pretend that you alone bear the consequences.
Those close to you have no automatic veto.
But neither are they people outside the expedition's plans who need only deal with their emotions on their own.
The narrator says that those departing do not look at their mothers and wives because they fear the pain, and even a change in the firm purpose on which they have embarked.
This restraint is easy to understand.
No difficult undertaking can remain forever in repeated discussion.
At some point, the ships must leave port.
If every instance of weeping reopened the entire decision, many things requiring courage and sustained commitment could never begin.
Someone may also know that a farewell will weaken their resolve, and protect a carefully considered direction by refusing to look back.
Firmness is not inherently a rejection of others.
Sometimes it simply marks the point when action must finally move from thought to execution.
But a distinction still needs to be seen here:
I have heard your reasons and, having decided, will not keep wavering.
And
To preserve my decision, I avoid truly seeing your reasons.
These are not the same thing.
The poem does not tell us how each sailor previously discussed the voyage with his family.
Nor can their failure to look up establish that the entire expedition never underwent any collective judgment.
But this gesture shows at least one thing:
The relationships on shore still have the power to change the decision.
It is precisely because they have that power that eyes must be averted.
The more a shared mission needs to protect itself by not looking, not listening, and boarding quickly, the more it should acknowledge:
“Shared” does not mean that everyone has the same answer.
Some set out with resolve.
Some see them off in tears.
Some openly object.
Ultimately, the decision is carried out by those who can organize the fleet, allocate resources, and set sail.
A community can act without unanimity.
But without unanimity, it should not later portray everyone as having had a single will.
The old man asks:
Why seek far away what lies close at hand?
Why diminish your own country's population and weaken its strength, merely to acquire the name of master across the vast spaces of India, Persia, Arabia, and Ethiopia?
He also says that if glory is truly to be won through religion and war, longstanding enemies are already nearby. Why seek unfamiliar dangers?
This passage prevents us from simply recasting the old man as a modern pacifist.
He does not oppose all war.
Nor does he oppose the religious language of friends and enemies.
He merely considers distant expeditions more deluded and more draining for the country than wars close to home.
His world is still one of empire, religious conflict, and masculine public glory.
We therefore cannot make him speak fully for those who will later be conquered, or call him the poem's hidden modern anti-imperialist thinker.
He sees some of the costs.
He does not see them all.
This does not invalidate his dissent.
A person need not possess the most complete or most modern reasons to be entitled to point out problems in an undertaking at hand.
The old man may misjudge the benefits of an ocean voyage.
He may propose an equally dangerous alternative.
He may also divide the world into the friends and enemies of his own age.
But these limitations do not cancel the questions he raises:
What will the expedition consume?
Who will bear the burden?
Does “glory” pronounce the cost worthwhile before it has even been incurred?
Why must they go so far?
Is the country committing all its courage, wealth, and people to a direction that has yet to prove itself?
Examining a speaker's limitations must not become a way to avoid answering his questions.
Finally, the old man places the urge to sail within a group of ancient stories.
Prometheus brought fire to humankind, and fire also brought weapons, death, and desire into the world.
Phaethon tried to drive his father's sun chariot.
Icarus entered the sky with his father.
With fire, iron, water, heat, and cold, human beings keep attempting lofty and dangerous undertakings.
In his telling, crossing boundaries is almost always linked to disaster.
This is certainly too strong a claim.
If people never crossed the boundaries of the known, voyages, knowledge, and new ways of living together would never come about.
“No one has done it before” cannot be a reason never to do it.
Many capabilities later regarded as ordinary required uncertainty to be borne at the outset.
So the old man cannot prove that the expedition must be wrong merely by invoking failures in myth.
But his myths also remind us:
Loftiness is not automatically nobility.
The more an undertaking can stir the imagination, the easier it becomes to treat danger itself as proof of value.
As though only coming close to destruction could show that the undertaking is great enough.
The fleet will later complete the voyage celebrated by the epic.
Will that prove the old man wrong?
Success can refute some of his judgments.
If he says the expedition cannot possibly be completed, its completion disproves him.
If he says the sea holds only death, with no knowledge, routes, or national gains, the eventual outcome will also qualify his conclusions.
But success cannot be turned backward to mean:
Therefore, none of the risks before departure was worth raising.
Therefore, every death and separation was merely a reasonable price for success.
Therefore, those who took no part in the decision should have regarded the expedition as their highest value from the start.
An undertaking's success proves that it achieved certain goals.
It does not by itself prove that those goals were worth every cost, or that no less costly way of achieving them, with sounder limits, existed.
The outcome can revise an objection.
It cannot erase that objection from the past.
Perhaps what truly matters is not whether the old man was ultimately “right” or “wrong.”
It is that this epic celebrating the expedition did not remove him from the scene of departure.
The poem could easily have written only of flags, prayers, courage, and the sea.
It could have made the tears of mothers and wives mere decoration for a heroic farewell.
It could also have portrayed the old man's voice as ridiculous, timid, or feeble with age.
Instead, he is described as experienced, wise, and venerable in appearance.
His voice crosses the water and reaches those aboard.
The fleet still leaves.
But the prospect of victory does not drown out dissent.
This makes glory more than a single voice from the very beginning.
A community cannot wait for everyone's agreement before every public undertaking.
Some believe the risk is worth taking.
Some believe the resources should go elsewhere.
Some will benefit.
Some will lose.
In the end, a decision must be reached.
The real question is not how to eliminate disagreement.
It is whether, once the decision has been made, those on the losing side are still recognized as people within the community who have an answer to give.
Whether their reasons are recorded.
Whether the costs they bear are counted.
Whether, when the outcome later proves favorable, it is still possible to say:
This success has not made every earlier concern foolish.
The old man does not stop the fleet.
But the poem's preservation of his voice is itself a limit:
Those who prevail may sail.
They cannot monopolize what the voyage is called.
Who is entitled to say that a community's glory costs too much?
Letting only those aboard the ships speak is not enough.
They bear the dangers at sea, but not every consequence for those left behind.
Letting only the relatives on shore speak is not enough either.
They bear the loss, but need not carry through the direction the voyagers have affirmed.
Still less can rulers and epic poets have the only say.
They can organize a mission and preserve a reputation, but they do not necessarily participate in every death and separation in the same way.
Perhaps no single position can deliver the overall judgment.
Precisely for that reason, dissenting voices cannot be disqualified merely because they did not prevail in the decision.
They bring forward the part of the cost that those acting are most likely to overlook.
The voyagers do not look at their mothers and wives.
But the old man ensures that they still hear a voice from shore while at sea.
The arrangement is exact.
Eyes can be averted.
A voice still follows them aboard.
Resolute action need not stop because it hears objections.
But neither should it consider itself fulfilled only when it can hear none at all.
A mission that can truly answer for itself cannot preserve only the reasons that support it.
It must also know which relationships, which lives, and which futures have not made the same choice, yet will all be changed by the voyage.
The fleet continues out to sea.
The old man stays on shore.
He has not become captain or gained the final say.
Nor will the rest of the epic remain in Lisbon as he wishes.
But before all the glory of Portugal begins to be sung, the poem first preserves an unsuccessful “do not go.”
This means that no later victory can entirely forget:
At departure, someone asked whether fame dressed the cost too beautifully.
Someone asked whether distant gold and kingdoms were worth deaths and separations at home.
Someone asked who decides on an undertaking called the glory of a community, and who pays for it.
The old man did not stop the fleet.
What he did was make it impossible for glory ever again to say:
No one ever asked these questions.

*Textual basis: Luís de Camões, The Lusiads, Canto 4, stanzas 84—104. Stanzas 84—87 describe the fleet, youthful courage, the voyagers' preparation to face death, and religious prayer; stanzas 88—92 describe the city crowds and the tearful farewells of mothers, wives, old people, and children; in stanza 93, those departing do not raise their eyes to their mothers and wives, lest pain shake their settled purpose; stanza 94 describes an experienced, venerable-looking old man raising his voice so that those on the water can still hear him clearly; in stanzas 95—104, he attacks the desire for dominion named “fame,” “glory,” and “honor,” questions death, danger, the consumption of wealth, distant kingdoms and gold mines, urges that nearby religious enemies take priority, and invokes boundary-crossing in the stories of Prometheus, Phaethon, and Icarus. This essay does not make the old man the final spokesman for Camões or for the poem as a whole, nor does it modernize him into a pacifist or a comprehensive anti-imperialist voice. It asks only why an epic that still celebrates ocean voyaging permanently preserves a dissent that did not stop the undertaking at the scene of its departure.*
